cards.title: Ad Hominem
cards.notes: Attacking the person making the argument rather than the argument itself.

fields.Definition: Attacking the person making the argument rather than the argument itself.
fields.Example: "You can't trust his health advice — he's overweight."

cards.title: Straw Man
cards.notes: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack.

fields.Definition: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack.
fields.Example: "He wants stricter gun laws, so he wants to ban all guns."

cards.title: False Dichotomy
cards.notes: Presenting only two options as if no others exist.

fields.Definition: Presenting only two options as if no others exist.
fields.Example: "You're either with us or against us."

cards.title: Slippery Slope
cards.notes: Claiming one event will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without justification.

fields.Definition: Claiming one event will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without justification.
fields.Example: "If we allow same-sex marriage, next people will want to marry animals."

cards.title: Appeal to Authority
cards.notes: Using an authority figure's opinion as conclusive evidence regardless of relevance.

fields.Definition: Using an authority figure's opinion as conclusive evidence regardless of relevance.
fields.Example: "A famous actor says this supplement works, so it must."

cards.title: Circular Reasoning
cards.notes: Using the conclusion as a premise in the argument.

fields.Definition: Using the conclusion as a premise in the argument.
fields.Example: "The Bible is true because the Bible says it is true."

cards.title: Hasty Generalization
cards.notes: Drawing a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative examples.

fields.Definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative examples.
fields.Example: "I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there is rude."

cards.title: Post Hoc
cards.notes: Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B.

fields.Definition: Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B.
fields.Example: "I wore my lucky socks and we won — the socks caused the win."

cards.title: Appeal to Emotion
cards.notes: Using emotional manipulation in place of logical argument.

fields.Definition: Using emotional manipulation in place of logical argument.
fields.Example: "Think of the children — we must ban this immediately."

cards.title: Red Herring
cards.notes: Introducing irrelevant information to divert attention from the real issue.

fields.Definition: Introducing irrelevant information to divert attention from the real issue.
fields.Example: Deflecting a question about policy by discussing personal attacks on critics.

cards.title: Bandwagon
cards.notes: Claiming something is true or good because many people believe or do it.

fields.Definition: Claiming something is true or good because many people believe or do it.
fields.Example: "Millions of people can't be wrong — join us!"

cards.title: Appeal to Ignorance
cards.notes: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or vice versa.

fields.Definition: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or vice versa.
fields.Example: "No one has disproven ghosts exist, so they must."

cards.title: False Equivalence
cards.notes: Treating two unequal things as if they are morally or logically equivalent.

fields.Definition: Treating two unequal things as if they are morally or logically equivalent.
fields.Example: "Both sides have extremists, so both parties are equally bad."

cards.title: Equivocation
cards.notes: Exploiting a word's multiple meanings to mislead within an argument.

fields.Definition: Exploiting a word's multiple meanings to mislead within an argument.
fields.Example: "The sign said 'fine for parking here' — so I parked."

cards.title: Tu Quoque
cards.notes: Dismissing a claim by pointing out the other person's inconsistency rather than addressing the argument.

fields.Definition: Dismissing a claim by pointing out the other person's inconsistency rather than addressing the argument.
fields.Example: "Why should I stop smoking? You used to smoke too."

cards.title: Appeal to Nature
cards.notes: Arguing something is good because it is natural, or bad because it is artificial.

fields.Definition: Arguing something is good because it is natural, or bad because it is artificial.
fields.Example: "This medicine is synthetic, so it must be harmful."

cards.title: Anecdotal Evidence
cards.notes: Using a personal story or isolated example to support a broad claim.

fields.Definition: Using a personal story or isolated example to support a broad claim.
fields.Example: "My grandfather smoked a pack a day and lived to 95, so smoking isn't that dangerous."

cards.title: No True Scotsman
cards.notes: Redefining a group's criteria to exclude inconvenient counterexamples.

fields.Definition: Redefining a group's criteria to exclude inconvenient counterexamples.
fields.Example: "No true Scotsman would put sugar on porridge." [After told a Scotsman does]

cards.title: Gambler's Fallacy
cards.notes: Believing past independent random events affect the probability of future ones.

fields.Definition: Believing past independent random events affect the probability of future ones.
fields.Example: "The coin has come up heads five times — tails is due."

cards.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
cards.notes: Continuing a losing course of action because of past investment rather than future value.

fields.Definition: Continuing a losing course of action because of past investment rather than future value.
fields.Example: "I've already spent so much on this project, I can't quit now."

cards.title: Loaded Question
cards.notes: Asking a question with a harmful or false assumption embedded in it.

fields.Definition: Asking a question with a harmful or false assumption embedded in it.
fields.Example: "Have you stopped cheating on your taxes?"

cards.title: False Cause
cards.notes: Incorrectly identifying the cause of an event or correlation as causation.

fields.Definition: Incorrectly identifying the cause of an event or correlation as causation.
fields.Example: "Ice cream sales rise with drowning rates — ice cream causes drowning."

cards.title: Appeal to Tradition
cards.notes: Assuming something is correct or better simply because it is older or traditional.

fields.Definition: Assuming something is correct or better simply because it is older or traditional.
fields.Example: "We've always done it this way — there's no need to change."

cards.title: Genetic Fallacy
cards.notes: Judging something as good or bad based on its origin rather than its actual content.

fields.Definition: Judging something as good or bad based on its origin rather than its actual content.
fields.Example: "That idea came from a discredited person, so it must be wrong."

cards.title: Moving the Goalposts
cards.notes: Changing the criteria for a claim after it has been met, to avoid conceding the point.

fields.Definition: Changing the criteria for a claim after it has been met, to avoid conceding the point.
fields.Example: "OK, you found one study — show me ten more." [After one was the original demand]
